# Court Cases and Bill of Rights Part 2

## By the end of today

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
You will be able to explain incorporation, the core criminal-procedure cases, and how speech and civil-rights landmarks defend a prior consensus against a current majority.
:::

## Where this fits

Last week: why a democracy needs a countermajoritarian court.

Today: the cases that make that real.

## Remember Barron

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
In 1833 the Bill of Rights bound the federal government, not the states.
:::

## Then the 14th Amendment

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.5em;"}
Due process and equal protection gave the Court a door to apply most of those rights to the states.
:::

## Incorporation is not a slogan

Most of the Bill of Rights now binds the states.

Not all of it. Not all at once.

## Mapp v. Ohio (1961)

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Illegally seized evidence is out of a state prosecution.
:::

## Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
If the state can take your liberty, it must supply counsel when you cannot.
:::

## Miranda v. Arizona (1966)

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Custodial interrogation requires a warning before the state uses your words.
:::

## Particularity, again

"Seize anything related to the investigation" is not a particular description.

A searchable plate warehouse, queried later, has the same shape.

## Speech is not unlimited

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Brandenburg: punish speech directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.
:::

Advocacy of ugly ideas is not enough.

## Press

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.5em;"}
Prior restraint is the exception. After-the-fact liability is the ordinary tool.
:::

## Plessy to Brown

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Separate-but-equal was the 1896 settlement. Brown withdrew it.
:::

## Loving v. Virginia (1967)

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
A majority may not use marriage law to sort people by race.
:::

## Texas note

Texas has two high courts.

Criminal-procedure fights often end at the Court of Criminal Appeals before they ever reach the U.S. Supreme Court.

## Recap

- Incorporation is how paper rights reach state force
- Mapp, Gideon, Miranda are the enforcement tools
- Speech tests narrowed; civil-rights cases expanded who counts
- Dual high courts are the Texas fork in the same road

## Top Hat

- T/F: Barron held that the Bill of Rights originally bound the states.
- MC: Gideon is best described as incorporating the right to:
- T/F: Brandenburg allows the state to punish any speech that praises violence.
- Likert: "The exclusionary rule protects rights more than it rewards the guilty."
